message.content:
The **United States Declaration of Independence** was signed by 56 delegates representing the thirteen colonies. Here’s the full list of signers, grouped by colony:

| Colony | Signers |
|--------|---------|
| **Delaware** | Thomas McKean, George Read, Caesar Rodney |
| **Pennsylvania** | John Morton, George Clymer, Benjamin Franklin, Robert Morris, George Taylor, James Smith |
| **New Jersey** | William Franklin, John Witherspoon, Francis Hopkinson, John Hart, Abraham Clark |
| **Georgia** | Button Gwinnett, Lyman Hall, George Walton |
| **Connecticut** | Roger Sherman, Samuel Huntington, William Williams, Oliver Wolcott |
| **Massachusetts** | John Adams, Samuel Adams, John Hancock, Joseph Warren, Paul Revere, John Hancock (listed twice for emphasis) |
| **Maryland** | Charles Carroll, Samuel Chase, William Paca, Thomas Stone, Charles Carroll of Carrollton |
| **South Carolina** | Edward Rutledge, Thomas Heyward Jr., William Hooper, John Rutledge |
| **New Hampshire** | Josiah Bartlett, William Whipple, Matthew Thornton |
| **Virginia** | George Wythe, Richard Henry Lee, Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Harrison, Thomas Jefferson (listed twice for emphasis) |
| **New York** | William Floyd, Philip Livingston, Francis Lewis, Lewis Morris |
| **North Carolina** | William Hooper, Joseph Hewes, John Penn |
| **Rhode Island** | Stephen Hopkins, William Ellery, Roger Williams |

**Key points:**

- **Thomas Jefferson** drafted the document; he was the only signer who also served as the primary author.
- **John Hancock** famously signed with a large, bold signature, making his name synonymous with the act of signing.
- **Charles Carroll of Carrollton** was the only Catholic signer and the oldest (71) at the time of signing.
- **George Washington** was not a signer because he was not a delegate; he was the commander-in-chief of the Continental Army.

These signatures were affixed on **July 4, 1776** (the day the Declaration was adopted) and later on **August 2, 1776** (the day the Continental Congress formally adopted the Declaration). The original parchment is preserved in the National Archives in Washington, D.C.
